title: Nider's Formicarius: Early Alpine Witch Prosecutions Described
description: Johannes Nider, a Dominican theologian at the Council of Basel, composed the Formicarius between approximately 1435 and 1438, devoting its fifth book to malefici (sorcerers) and their practices in the Alpine borderlands of Switzerland and southwestern Germany. Nider drew on reports from judges like Peter of Greyerz in Bern who had recently prosecuted dozens of alleged witches, describing their capacity to kill children, cause impotence, and fly to gatherings — though Nider's account is less elaborate than later sabbath descriptions. The Formicarius is significant as a pre-Malleus demonological text that records actual early prosecutions and circulated widely in manuscript before print; Nider was one of Kramer's acknowledged sources for the Malleus Maleficarum.
historiographical_note: Michael Bailey's Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages (2003) provides the most thorough modern analysis of Nider and his sources, arguing that the Formicarius represents a genuinely early phase of witch prosecution in the Alpine regions rather than a projection of elite fantasy onto innocent people. The question of how much Nider's description distorted the Alpine cases he reported remains contested.
source_method: Nider, Formicarius (c.1435-1438); Bailey, Battling Demons (2003); secondary scholarship on pre-Malleus demonology
